common_name: Dacotah Switchgrass (Short-Statured Northern Plains Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Dacotah was collected in 1935 near Breien, North Dakota, and developed by USDA-ARS Mandan with the Bismarck, ND Plant Materials Center specifically for climates as cold as North Dakota and Minnesota.

directions: Dacotah is a distinctly short-statured switchgrass release bred for the Northern Great Plains, staying half the height of lowland switchgrass cultivars like Kanlow or Alamo while retaining the species' deep, drought-proof root system. It was jointly released by the North Dakota and Minnesota Agricultural Experiment Stations with USDA-ARS and the Bismarck Plant Materials Center, chosen specifically for reliable winter survival and earlier maturity in climates too cold for southern-source switchgrass. Its compact size and dense, fine-textured summer foliage make it useful for erosion control on rangeland and roadside plantings as well as a tidier switchgrass option for small northern gardens that lack room for taller cultivars. Cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in early spring before new growth resumes.
sources: USDA NRCS Bismarck Plant Materials Center, North Dakota
USDA-ARS Northern Great Plains Research Laboratory, Mandan, ND
North Dakota State University Extension

common_name: Rountree Big Bluestem (Iowa-Missouri Forage and Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to average soil in full sun; Rountree was collected from a native stand near Moorhead in Monona County, Iowa, and selected and increased at the Elsberry, Missouri Plant Materials Center for release with the Missouri Agricultural Experiment Station.

directions: Rountree was bred to improve on older big bluestem releases with a faster seedling growth rate, better resistance to leaf rust, superior forage production, and greater resistance to lodging in wind and rain. It matures at about the same time as Pawnee, roughly twelve days ahead of Kaw, giving Iowa and Missouri gardeners a slightly earlier turkeyfoot seed-head display than the Flint Hills selections. Beyond its original role as pasture forage, it is widely used in environmental plantings for erosion control and prairie restoration, and its upright, blue-green clumps colored copper-bronze in fall make a sturdy vertical accent in a native landscape border. Cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in early spring before new growth begins.
sources: USDA NRCS Elsberry Plant Materials Center, Missouri
Missouri Agricultural Experiment Station
Iowa State University Extension

common_name: Iuka Eastern Gamagrass (Southern Plains Wildlife and Forage Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Iuka traces to a 21-plant selection made in 1979 from over 500 eastern gamagrass accessions collected by USDA-ARS's Southern Plains Range Research Station in Woodward, Oklahoma, from Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, and Arkansas, and was released through the Grass Variety Review Board in 1995.

directions: Iuka is a Southern Plains eastern gamagrass selection bred from a broad, multi-state collection of wild accessions rather than a single parent, giving it strong regional adaptation across Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, and Arkansas. Dense clumps of wide, corn-like leaves produce jointed summer seed spikes bearing large, hard seeds that are a preferred food of wild turkey, quail, and other upland game, and the vigorous, protein-rich forage doubles as productive pasture in areas managed for wildlife. Like other eastern gamagrass selections it establishes slowly in its first year or two while its deep root system develops, then persists for decades as a bold-textured, low-maintenance clump ideal for moist meadow edges and rain garden borders. Cut clumps back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.
sources: USDA-ARS Southern Plains Range Research Station, Woodward, Oklahoma
USDA NRCS Plant Materials Program — Eastern Gamagrass Plant Guide
Oklahoma State University Extension

common_name: El Reno Sideoats Grama (Historic Southern Plains Conservation Selection)

planting.note: Sow directly after last frost into prepared, weed-free soil at a light 1/4-inch depth; El Reno was collected in 1934 from a field near El Reno, Oklahoma, and released cooperatively in 1944 by the Manhattan, Kansas Plant Materials Center and the Kansas Agricultural Experiment Station, making it one of the oldest NRCS grass releases still in commerce.

directions: El Reno stands out among sideoats grama releases for its vigor, dense leafiness, and long field-proven reliability across eight decades of use in Southern Plains pasture and conservation seedings. Unlike some wild bunch-type ecotypes, it spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form a loose sod, giving it useful erosion-control value on slopes and disturbed ground. Distinctive arching flower stems bear small oat-like seed clusters that all hang from one side of the stem, turning orange-tan in fall and persisting into winter for continued garden interest. It thrives in hot, dry, rocky, or sandy soils and needs no irrigation or fertilizer once established.
sources: USDA NRCS Manhattan Plant Materials Center, Kansas
Kansas Agricultural Experiment Station
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Sideoats Grama

common_name: Hachita Blue Grama (Drought-Resistant Southwest Rangeland Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in well-drained to dry soil in full sun after last frost, or in late summer for fall establishment; Hachita was collected in 1957 about 32 miles south of Hachita Mountain in southern New Mexico and developed at the Los Lunas Plant Materials Center as accession NM-118.

directions: Hachita was selected specifically for greater drought resistance than other blue grama sources, tracing to a semi-desert plains site at 4,400 feet elevation receiving only about 10 inches of annual precipitation. It is widely used for rangeland improvement, mine-spoil reclamation, and roadside stabilization across the semiarid Southwest, and its unusual curved, comb-like seed heads on wiry stems give it strong ornamental value in a low-water native lawn substitute or xeric garden planting. It forms a fine-textured, low, blue-green turf and is highly resistant to deer browsing. Leave seed heads standing through winter for maximum wildlife and ornamental value.
sources: USDA NRCS Los Lunas Plant Materials Center, New Mexico
New Mexico State University Agricultural Experiment Station
Colorado State University Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Lovington Blue Grama (High-Yield Eastern New Mexico Rangeland Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Lovington was collected in 1944 near Lovington, New Mexico on loamy upland rangeland and released in 1963 by the Los Lunas Plant Materials Center with the New Mexico State University Agricultural Science Center.

directions: Lovington produces about 15 percent more forage than unimproved blue grama strains in both cultivated and range plantings, a trait that also translates into denser, more vigorous garden stands. It is recommended for eastern New Mexico and southeastern Colorado where annual precipitation reaches 12 inches or more, and it later served as a parent source for the subsequent 'Alma' blue grama release. Wiry stems carry the species' signature curved, eyelash-shaped seed heads from midsummer through fall, and established plants tolerate extended drought without supplemental water. It works well as a low-water native turf alternative or mixed into a shortgrass prairie wildflower planting.
sources: USDA NRCS Los Lunas Plant Materials Center, New Mexico
New Mexico State University Agricultural Science Center
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Blue Grama

common_name: Rodan Western Wheatgrass (Northern Plains Drought-Tolerant Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Drill into a firm, weed-free seedbed in late fall or early spring at a shallow 1/2 to 1 inch depth; Rodan originated from a 70-acre field of western wheatgrass in the Missouri River bottoms near Mandan, North Dakota, and was released in 1983 by USDA-ARS, NRCS, and the North Dakota Agricultural Experiment Station.

directions: Rodan is a strongly rhizomatous western wheatgrass selected for drought tolerance, leafiness, and forage vigor, outyielding other western wheatgrass cultivars by an average of 178 pounds per acre of forage across 58 replicated trials. Its thinner, less heavily veined leaves than older cultivars give it a softer texture, and it forms a tight, erosion-resistant sod under dryland conditions. It is best suited to the northern Plains, including the western Dakotas and eastern Montana and Wyoming, where it is used for rangeland restoration, roadside stabilization, and reclamation of disturbed soils. Avoid grazing or mowing until the second season while the rhizome network establishes.
sources: USDA-ARS and NRCS, Mandan, North Dakota
North Dakota State Agricultural Experiment Station
USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Western Wheatgrass

common_name: Rosana Western Wheatgrass (Northern Great Plains Reclamation Grass)

planting.note: Drill into a firm, weed-free seedbed in late fall or early spring; Rosana was collected in 1959 from native meadows along Porcupine Creek near Forsyth, Montana, and released in 1972 by the Bridger Plant Materials Center with the Montana Agricultural Experiment Station.

directions: Rosana was selected for seedling vigor and ease of establishment, spreading by slender, creeping rhizomes into a dense, shallow, fibrous root system while deeper roots reach down as far as five feet for exceptional drought resilience. It is recommended for reseeding depleted rangeland and reclaiming disturbed land across the Northern Great Plains and Intermountain regions, establishing reliably from either late-fall or early-spring seedings without the need for added fertilizer. Its blue-green color persists through summer heat, and it pairs naturally with native prairie legumes such as purple prairie clover in conservation seed mixes. Rosana is similar in adaptation to the later-released Rodan but performs best on finer-textured soils in slightly lower-rainfall areas.
sources: USDA NRCS Bridger Plant Materials Center, Montana
Montana Agricultural Experiment Station
USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Western Wheatgrass

common_name: Riley Partridge Pea (Kansas Wildlife and Pollinator Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow scarified or soaked seed after last frost in poor, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Riley was first released as a source-identified germplasm in 1999 and formally released as a cultivar in 2007 by the Manhattan, Kansas Plant Materials Center.

directions: Riley is a Kansas-sourced partridge pea selected for superior performance in critical area seeding, roadside plantings, and wildlife habitat improvement, and it is recommended for park and recreational area beautification as well. As a nitrogen-fixing native annual legume it produces cheerful yellow flowers from midsummer through fall that draw bumblebees and other native pollinators, and its seed remains a major winter food source for northern bobwhite and other quail because it holds up well through cold weather. Do not enrich the planting soil, since excess fertility reduces flowering, and expect it to self-sow abundantly once established. Plant in sweeps of at least 10 to 20 plants for the best wildlife and pollinator impact.
sources: USDA NRCS Manhattan Plant Materials Center, Kansas
USDA NRCS Plant Release Notice — Riley Partridge Pea
Kansas State University Extension

common_name: Cuero Purple Prairie Clover (South Texas Pollinator and Wildlife Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow scarified seed in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Cuero Germplasm was collected in 1970 from native plants in DeWitt County, Texas near the town of Cuero, and released in 2003 by the James E. "Bud" Smith Plant Materials Center in Knox City, Texas.

directions: Cuero is a warm-climate, south Texas-adapted source of purple prairie clover, selected for well-drained sites across south, central, and west Texas where average precipitation runs around 34 inches. From June through September it produces the species' distinctive cylindrical, thimble-like flower spikes densely packed with magenta-purple blooms that open progressively up the head, drawing an outsized diversity of native bees including several Dalea specialists. It is used in wildlife habitat and range plantings, perennial food plots, wildflower mixes, and pollinator habitat restoration, and as a nitrogen-fixing legume it improves soil fertility wherever it is seeded. Like other purple prairie clover sources it develops a deep taproot quickly and should be sown in its permanent location rather than transplanted.
sources: USDA NRCS James E. "Bud" Smith Plant Materials Center, Knox City, Texas
USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Purple Prairie Clover
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension

common_name: Wytana Fourwing Saltbush (Northern Plains Wildlife Browse Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in spring or fall in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Wytana was released in 1976 by the Bridger, Montana Plant Materials Center and is a natural cross between fourwing saltbush and Gardner's saltbush (Atriplex gardneri). It is dioecious — plant several seedlings to ensure both male and female shrubs for seed set.

directions: Wytana is a shorter, more herbaceous-natured fourwing saltbush than the typical species, bred for the colder Great Plains and mountain foothill climates of Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming where taller southern-source saltbush struggles to overwinter. Its lower stature makes it easier to mechanically harvest for seed while still providing valuable browse and winter cover for pronghorn, mule deer, and upland game birds. Gray-green, slightly mealy foliage tolerates alkaline and saline soils poorly suited to most shrubs, and the shrub remains a standard NRCS conservation practice component in North and South Dakota plantings. It needs no irrigation once established and tolerates repeated browsing or shearing.
sources: USDA NRCS Bridger Plant Materials Center, Montana
USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Fourwing Saltbush
Montana Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Marana Fourwing Saltbush (Southwest Desert Wildlife Cover Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in spring or fall in well-drained, sandy to clay-loam soil in full sun; Marana was collected in 1961 near El Cajon in San Diego County, California, and released in 1979 by the NRCS Plant Materials Center in Lockeford, California.

directions: Marana was selected specifically for ease of establishment and drought resistance and is best adapted to southern New Mexico, southern Arizona, and southern to central California. It is valued for critical-area plantings on sandy to clay-loam, well-drained soils, providing upland game bird cover and environmental enhancement where few other shrubs will establish. Like other fourwing saltbush selections it is dioecious, with the distinctive four-winged papery seed capsules forming on female shrubs in fall as an important food source for pronghorn, mule deer, and quail. Gray-green foliage is moderately salt-tolerant, making it useful along roadsides treated with de-icing salt as well as in low-water desert landscaping.
sources: USDA NRCS Lockeford Plant Materials Center, California
USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Fourwing Saltbush
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Direct sow in spring or fall in well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Rincon originated near Canjilon in Rio Arriba County, New Mexico, at roughly 7,800 feet elevation, developed by NRCS for higher, colder sites than most fourwing saltbush releases.

directions: Rincon is an erect, leafy fourwing saltbush form notable for early-season green-up, giving wildlife access to nutritious browse earlier in spring than later-greening selections. It is best adapted to higher, colder sites across central Utah, central Nevada, western Colorado, and central New Mexico, filling a niche among NRCS fourwing saltbush releases alongside the lower-elevation Marana and the northern-plains Wytana. As with other fourwing saltbush, it is dioecious and produces papery, four-winged seed capsules on female shrubs that are heavily used by pronghorn, mule deer, and upland birds through fall and winter. It tolerates alkaline soils and extended drought once established and needs no supplemental irrigation.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Fourwing Saltbush
USDA NRCS Plant Materials Program, Southwest region
New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

common_name: Maple Grove Lewis Flax (Intermountain Pollinator and Erosion-Control Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow in spring or fall on well-drained soil, pressing seed in lightly; Maple Grove was collected at Maple Grove campground in central Utah and released in 2003 by the USDA Forest Service Shrub Sciences Laboratory with the Aberdeen, Idaho Plant Materials Center, selected for vigor, floral display, and competitiveness when seeded with grasses.

directions: Maple Grove opens clear sky-blue flowers each morning atop slender, wiry stems from a native Utah collection selected specifically for beauty as well as function, making it one of the more ornamental NRCS conservation releases. It was bred to hold its own in seeding mixtures alongside competitive grasses, a trait that makes it valuable in erosion-control and reclamation seedings across the Intermountain West as well as in pollinator wildflower mixes, where its abundant blooms draw native bees throughout the growing season. Once established it is remarkably drought tolerant and self-sows readily to form long-lived drifts. Deadhead spent flower stalks only if reseeding is not desired; otherwise allow seed to scatter for naturalizing.
sources: USDA Forest Service Shrub Sciences Laboratory
USDA NRCS Aberdeen Plant Materials Center, Idaho
USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Blue Flax / Lewis Flax

common_name: Reno Germplasm Illinois Bundleflower (Central Plains Wildlife and Forage Selection)

planting.note: Scarify seed and broadcast or drill in spring into a firm, well-prepared seedbed in full sun; Reno Germplasm was collected in 1974 by the Kansas Game and Parks Commission near Lake Cheney in Reno County, Kansas, and evaluated against 'Sabine' Illinois bundleflower at the Manhattan, Kansas Plant Materials Center before release.

directions: Reno Germplasm was selected on the basis of winter hardiness, plant persistence, and clipping response, making it a more cold-adapted choice for the Central Plains Region than the Texas-sourced 'Sabine' release it was compared against. Fine, fern-like, mimosa-type foliage and small white puffball flowers appear through summer, followed by the distinctive round, bristly seed clusters that give the species its common name and are heavily used by upland game birds and songbirds through fall and winter. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it improves soil fertility wherever it is seeded and is used in rangeland, critical area, and recreational area plantings across Kansas and neighboring states. It establishes slowly in its first season while building a deep taproot, then persists for many years without replanting.
sources: USDA NRCS Manhattan Plant Materials Center, Kansas
Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks
USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Illinois Bundleflower
